1156.title: The first way (ST I.2.3)
1156.hook: change needs a source that isn't itself changed
1156.howItsDone: Catholic philosophy courses often begin Thomas's five ways with the argument from motion, reading his hand-and-staff chain as what moves things now, not a first moment in time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, can we prove God? Reason can reach that God is, not all that God is. Your line was reason can reach.

A pot of water sits on the stove. Cold. It could be hot; it just isn't yet. Then the burner catches, and slowly the could-be becomes is. Small bubbles, then a rolling boil. The water didn't heat itself. Something already hot had to do it. That's almost too plain to say. But Thomas Aquinas builds his first argument for God on exactly that. In the Summa he calls it the more obvious way, because it starts from something nobody can miss: things change. Today's word is that first way.
screen: `COLD WATER ON THE STOVE.` → `IT DIDN'T HEAT ITSELF.` → `THINGS CHANGE.`

segments.voice: First, a word: motion. For Thomas it means any change, a could-be becoming an is. Cold water getting hot. A seed becoming a tree. Second, the rule. Nothing gets from could-be to is on its own; it needs something that already is. Thomas's example is fire: fire, actually hot, makes wood, which could be hot, actually hot. And the same thing can't be giving and receiving the same heat at once. So whatever is changed is changed by another. Third, the chain. Thomas pictures a hand moving a staff, and the staff moving something else. The staff moves only because the hand moves it. Suppose every link were like the staff, only passing along motion it got elsewhere, with no source anywhere. Then nothing would move at all. A thousand sticks and no hand push nothing. So, Thomas says, we must come to a first mover, moved by no other, and this everyone understands to be God. Thomas isn't walking back through time to a first push at the start of the world. Later in the Summa he says reason alone can't prove the world had a beginning; that is held by faith. His example points to a chain right now, like hand and staff. And unmoved doesn't mean frozen, like a statue. It means God has no could-be left; nothing in God is waiting to become. The letter of James says it, in the Douay-Rheims: the Father of lights, "with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration."
screen: `MOTION MEANS ANY CHANGE.` · `NOTHING CHANGES ITSELF.` · `NO HAND, NO MOVING STAFF.` · `A CHAIN NOW, NOT A FIRST PUSH.` · then, large: `NO CHANGE, NOR SHADOW OF ALTERATION.`

segments.voice: Find one moving thing, a curtain in a draft, steam from a cup, your own chest rising and falling, and watch it without naming anything. Then ask what's moving it, and what's moving that, one link back at a time, each one leaning on something else. If you pray, rest at the end of the chain with the one Thomas calls the first mover; if you don't, just keep watching it move.
The first way. Thomas's argument from change: whatever changes is changed by another, and the chain must rest on a first mover, moved by nothing.
Your line: the unmoved mover. Not a push long ago, but a source right now. Until tomorrow.

1157.title: The second and third ways
1157.hook: causes and contingent things point to a first cause and a necessary being
1157.howItsDone: Catholic philosophy courses often read the second and third ways together, the arguments from causes and from contingent things, and discuss where the third way's reasoning is contested.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first way: the chain of change rests on one moved by nothing. Your line was the unmoved mover.

At a family dinner, an old couple tells their story again. She nearly didn't go to the dance that night. Rain, a sore throat, a cousin who talked her into it at the last minute. Everyone laughs. Then a granddaughter goes quiet, doing the math. If Grandma had stayed home, I wouldn't be here. A whole person, hanging on a cousin and the weather. Thomas Aquinas follows that thought further. Not only, why am I here? But, why is there anything at all? Today's word: the second and third ways.
screen: `SHE NEARLY STAYED HOME.` → `THEN I WOULDN'T BE HERE.` → `WHY IS THERE ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: The second way is a cousin of yesterday's. Yesterday was change; today is being made at all. Thomas finds in the world an order of causes. A lamp shines because current reaches it. The current runs because something drives it. Nothing can cause itself, he says, because it would have to exist before itself, which is impossible. And in an ordered line of causes, take away the first and you take away the rest: no first cause, no middle ones, no last one. But there are causes, here, working. So there is a first cause, to which, Thomas says, everyone gives the name of God. The third way goes deeper, into the granddaughter's question. Some things can be, and can also not be. Flowers. Mountains, slowly. People. They come to be and pass away. They don't have to exist. Then a bold step. If everything were like that, at some point there could have been nothing at all. And from nothing, nothing begins. So there would be nothing now. But there is something. So not everything can be the borrowing kind. Something must exist of itself, not lent its being by anything else, and giving being to the rest. This, Thomas says, all speak of as God. Readers argue over that bold middle step; we'll come back to it tomorrow. Scripture says the giving part plainly. In Acts, in the Douay-Rheims, Paul says God is "he who giveth to all life, and breath, and all things." Every borrowed thing, on this view, is borrowing from someone.

segments.voice: Choose one thing near you, a mug, a sparrow, your own hand on your knee, and say quietly: this didn't have to be. Let the surprise sink in for a few breaths, then take a second thing and a third, without hurrying toward an answer. If you pray, thank God that anything is here at all; if you don't, just let the question stand.
The second and third ways. Thomas's arguments from causes and from things that can fail to be: nothing makes itself, so there's a first cause, and something that exists of itself.

1158.title: The fourth and fifth ways
1158.hook: degrees of goodness and order in nature; thinkers still argue about these
1158.howItsDone: In Catholic classrooms the five ways are often taught as a set, with time given to the objections raised against them and to Thomas's own replies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second and third ways: a first cause, and something that exists of itself. Your line was why anything at all.

An arrow leaves the bow and crosses the whole field into the center of the target. The arrow knows nothing. It doesn't aim. It doesn't want the bullseye. And yet, from a good archer's hand, it gets there. That arrow is Thomas Aquinas's own picture, the last image in his five ways. Two are left. Today, walk them, then ask what an argument like this is for. Today's word: the fourth and fifth ways.
screen: `AN ARROW THAT DOESN'T AIM.` → `TWO WAYS LEFT.` → `WHAT IS AN ARGUMENT FOR?`

segments.voice: The fourth way starts from more and less. We call one act kinder than another, one answer truer, one life nobler. Thomas says more and less only make sense measured against a most. So there is something truest, best, noblest, and so most fully being, which causes the being and goodness in everything else. This, he says, we call God. His example shows his age: fire, the hottest thing, causing heat in all the rest. That's the science he learned. The point he's after is goodness, not fire. The fifth way is the arrow. Things without minds still act for an end. An acorn heads for oak. Rain falls, plants turn toward light, regularly, not by luck. But a thing with no mind can't head for a goal unless someone with a mind directs it, as the archer directs the arrow. So there is someone intelligent who directs natural things to their ends. This, he says, we call God. Notice what it's not: it isn't about how intricate a thing is, but how reliably mindless things lean toward a goal. The Psalm sings the same direction, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God." Now the arguing. Thomas meant these as real arguments, and readers, believing and not, still push on them: on the step from more to most, on whether nature's regularity needs a director. But Thomas called them ways. A way doesn't drag you. You walk it, weigh each step, and decide. He wrote them for beginners, in a book that states the other side first. An argument, for him, is an invitation to think, not a fist.
screen: `MORE AND LESS NEED A MOST.` · `MINDLESS THINGS ACT FOR AN END.` · `NOT INTRICACY, BUT DIRECTION.` · `A WAY HAS TO BE WALKED.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS SHEW FORTH THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Choose an argument you disagree with, about God or anything that matters, and walk it step by step, asking at each one whether it holds for you, until you find the exact step where you get off. Don't argue back; just notice that the argument can't make you do anything, only invite. If you pray, ask for an honest mind; if you don't, simply look at the spot where you stepped off.
The fourth and fifth ways. Thomas's arguments from degrees of goodness, which point to a most, and from order in nature, which points to a mind that directs.

segments.voice: Your line: arguments invite, not force. A way has to be walked. See you tomorrow.

1159.title: God is simple (ST I.3)
1159.hook: God has no parts; his being and his essence are one
1159.howItsDone: Catholic theology teaches divine simplicity as part of the doctrine of God, and readers of the Summa meet it right after the five ways, in the Summa's third question.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth and fifth ways: degrees of goodness, and an arrow that doesn't aim. Your line was arguments invite, not force.

A kid with a screwdriver has the back off an old radio on the kitchen floor. Screws in a saucer. A circuit board. A speaker cone. Wires in four colors. He's learning what grown-ups know: open almost anything and you find pieces. A sandwich is pieces. A song is notes. A sentence is words. You are a body and a breath, habits and moods, a past and a plan. So here's the question Thomas Aquinas asks right after the five ways: if God is, what is God made of? His answer is today's word.
screen: `A RADIO ON THE KITCHEN FLOOR.` → `OPEN IT: PIECES.` → `WHAT IS GOD MADE OF?`

segments.voice: Thomas opens with a confession: we can't know what God is, only what God is not. So he works by taking things away. First, a body. God is not one. He leans on Jesus's words in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is a spirit." Then further: God isn't made of anything at all. No stuff plus shape. No pieces. And no add-ons. You have a good habit, maybe patience, but you are not your patience; you could lose it on a bad Monday and still be you. There's a gap between who you are and what you have. In God, Thomas says, there's no gap. God doesn't have goodness the way you have patience. Then the deepest step. For everything else, what it is and that it is are two different things. You can know what a unicorn is without it existing. Your being is lent. In God, Thomas says, the two are one: what God is, is to be. Why care? Because anything made of parts depends on its parts, and on whatever put them together. A God built of pieces would need a builder, and the first cause of the five ways can't be like that. So simplicity here doesn't mean plain, or easy to understand; Thomas reaches it the hard way, by saying what God is not. It means whole. Undivided. Nothing in God pulling against anything else in God. Some readers find that strange and cold at first. Others find it a rest. On Thomas's account, a God with no parts is a God who can't come apart.

segments.voice: Choose one thing only, a single breath, a candle flame, a smooth stone in your palm, and let everything else fall to the edges. If you pray, rest there before the God Thomas calls simple; if you don't, just stay with the one thing.
Simplicity. In Thomas Aquinas, not plainness but wholeness: God has no parts, and in God what God is and that God is are one.
Your line: no parts. Tomorrow, how anyone can talk about a God like that. Rest well.

1160.title: Talking about God (ST I.13)
1160.hook: God is good, but not in exactly the way we are good
1160.howItsDone: Catholic theology uses Thomas's teaching on analogy to explain how words like good, wise and father can be said truly of God while God remains beyond them; readers meet it in the Summa's question on the names of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simplicity: God has no parts, nothing put together. Your line was no parts.

A girl back from her first trip to the coast is on the phone with an inland friend who's never seen the sea. It's like the lake, she says. But bigger. No, way bigger, you can't see the other side. And it moves by itself. And it's salty, and loud. She keeps reaching for words her friend already has, and every one is true, and every one falls short. Thomas Aquinas has the same problem, only harder. Every word we have, we learned from things around us. So what can good, or wise, mean of God? Today's word is his answer.
screen: `A GIRL DESCRIBES THE SEA.` → `LIKE THE LAKE, BUT BIGGER.` → `WHAT CAN OUR WORDS MEAN?`

segments.voice: Thomas sees two dead ends. The first: our words mean exactly the same of God as of us. God is good like a kind neighbor, just more so. But then God is one more thing among things, only larger, and yesterday Thomas said God isn't built like anything we know. The second: our words mean something totally different of God, the way a river bank and a savings bank share only a spelling. But then, Thomas says, we could know nothing about God, and every argument we've walked would be empty. So he takes a middle road, and calls it analogy. His example is healthy. A person is healthy. A meal is healthy, because it brings health. A face looks healthy, because it shows health. Same word, not the same meaning, and not unrelated either; each use points to the one health. God is good. Thomas insists this doesn't merely mean God causes good things, or isn't bad. Goodness is really in God, in a higher way. Then he flips the picture. We learn good from good things around us, so the word feels like ours first. But as to what it means, Thomas says, it belongs to God first, and to us by sharing. He points to Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, praying to the Father "of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named." We learned father from our fathers. Paul says fatherhood is named from God. So for Thomas, our words aren't wrong about God. They're true, and too small. God is like what they say, and more.
screen: `NOT THE SAME SENSE.` · `NOT A TOTALLY DIFFERENT SENSE.` · `LIKE THE WORD HEALTHY.` · `GOD'S FIRST, OURS BY SHARING.` · then, large: `OF WHOM ALL PATERNITY IS NAMED.`

segments.voice: Pick one word you'd use of God, or of whatever is largest in your life, good, faithful, father, light, and remember where you first learned it: a person, a morning, a kitchen. Analogy. Thomas Aquinas's way of speaking of God: our words are not used in exactly the same sense, nor a totally different one, but a related one.

1161.title: He who is (ST I.13.11)
1161.hook: the best name for God is he who is, being itself
1161.howItsDone: Catholic theology, following Thomas, often speaks of God as being itself, and Catholics hear the name from the burning bush in the readings at Mass when Exodus 3 is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, analogy: our words for God are true, and too small. Your line was like, and more.

A shepherd stands barefoot on a mountainside in front of a bush that burns and is not burned up. A voice has just told him to go back to Egypt and bring his people out. Moses has a practical worry. When I tell them the God of their fathers sent me, they'll ask his name. What do I say? The answer is a name that's barely a name at all. You first stood at this bush on day two hundred ninety-five. Now Thomas Aquinas asks which name for God fits best. Today's word is that name.
screen: `A BUSH THAT ISN'T BURNED UP.` → `WHAT IS HIS NAME?` → `A NAME THAT'S BARELY A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here is God's answer to Moses, in the Douay-Rheims: "I AM WHO AM." And then: "Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." Thomas asks whether He who is is the most fitting name for God. Yes, he says, for three reasons. First, what it means. Every other name names a kind of thing, or a quality. Rock. Shepherd. Wise. Good. This one names no kind at all. It names to be. And two days ago, Thomas said that in God, what God is and that God is are one. So a name that means simply is fits as no other does. Second, how open it is. Other names narrow God to one side; this one sets no edge. Thomas quotes an earlier teacher, John Damascene: this name holds being itself like a sea without limit or bound. Remember the girl who couldn't see the other side. Third, the tense. Not he who was. Not he who will be. He who is. Following Augustine, Thomas says there is no past or future in God. The name is always now. Then, careful as ever, a turn. In another respect, he says, the name God, and the holy name written in the Hebrew Bible, are more proper still, because they name God alone. No single name holds God; each catches something. That's analogy, carried all the way. But Thomas keeps a special place for this one: the name that points not at something God has, but at what God is.

1162.title: Creation, every moment (ST I.104)
1162.hook: God doesn't just start the world; he holds it in being now
1162.howItsDone: Catholics profess God as creator of heaven and earth in the Creed at Mass, and teachers in the tradition of Thomas often explain creation as God's ongoing gift of being, not only a first event.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he who is: Thomas says the fittest name for God is the one given at the burning bush. Your line was being itself.

A lamp is on in a room at night. Switch it off and the room goes dark at once; the light doesn't linger out of habit. A room is lit only while something shines into it. It's easy to hear creation as an event far back: a first morning, God starting things up and then, maybe, stepping back to watch them run. Thomas Aquinas thought that picture leaves out what matters most. Today's word is creation, in the present tense.
screen: `A ROOM LIT ONLY WHILE LIGHT SHINES.` → `CREATION: A FIRST MORNING?` → `THOMAS: THE PRESENT TENSE.`

segments.voice: In the Summa, Thomas asks whether creatures need God to keep them in being. His answer: yes, every creature, every moment. His image is the sun and the air. The air is bright while the sun shines on it; the brightness isn't something the air owns. Take the sun away and the air is dark. So it is, he says, between God and everything that exists. A house keeps standing after the builder goes home, because the builder only arranged bricks that were already there. God doesn't arrange what was already there. He gives things their being, and no creature can hold that up by itself. Thomas cites Augustine: if the Creator's power ever stopped, all things would stop with it. Remember from the first way: reason alone, Thomas says, can't prove the world had a beginning in time. He holds that it did, by faith. So creation, for him, is first of all not a date. It's dependence: being held. And keeping things in being isn't a second act God adds later. It's the same act that gives being, simply continuing. Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, speaks of Christ "upholding all things by the word of his power." And Paul tells the Athenians: "For in him we live, and move, and are." Put this beside yesterday. If God is being itself, everything else has its being from him, not once, but now. The chair under you. Your hands. The person who annoyed you this morning. Not wound up and left running. Held.

segments.voice: Feel the weight of your body on the chair or the floor: something is holding you up, and it isn't you. Go one layer deeper, to your being here at all, breath arriving unasked, a heart keeping its own time. If you pray, say the line from Acts slowly, in him we live, and move, and are; if you don't, simply rest in the fact that this moment was handed to you.
Creation. For Thomas, not only a beginning long ago, but God giving everything its being, right now, the way the sun keeps the air bright. Today's word.
Your line: held now. The cup in your hand, another hand: each one held in being this very moment. That's the week.
